narrative:
The 2017 Boston Red Sox were a team that found its identity gradually, weathering early inconsistency before catching fire in the summer and ultimately falling short when the lights burned brightest in October. Opening the season at a modest 13-11 in April, Boston's defining early moment came from an unlikely source: Pablo Sandoval, the embattled third baseman whose tenure in Boston had been a saga of disappointment, delivered a three-run homer that briefly lit up Fenway and hinted at the unpredictable cast of characters who would shape the year. The bullpen, however, quickly proved to be a source of anxiety — Craig Kimbrel and others surrendered pivotal late-inning shots that would become a recurring storyline.

May and June brought steady, if unspectacular, winning baseball as Boston went 16-12 in each month. Role players like Chris Young and Jackie Bradley Jr. delivered timely hits, and the offense began to find its rhythm. But the shadow of a stumbling July — a 13-14 mark — loomed over any sense of momentum, with Kimbrel again allowing a crushing home run to Mike Napoli and the pitching staff showing its vulnerabilities. The team was winning enough to stay relevant but had not yet discovered the engine that would truly drive them.

August was the season's transformative month, a blazing 18-9 stretch that announced Boston as a genuine force. Christian Vázquez hit a stunning walk-off three-run homer against Cleveland, Mookie Betts roped a go-ahead double that swung a game by 0.808 win probability — the single most impactful regular-season play of the year — and newcomer Eduardo Núñez, acquired at the trade deadline, immediately made his presence felt with a clutch two-run double. Rafael Devers, the rookie third baseman, flashed his enormous potential, and Mitch Moreland came through repeatedly in the clutch. September carried that energy forward at a 17-10 clip, with Benintendi delivering a big three-run single to secure the division.

Then came October, and the Houston Astros. The ALDS exposed the Red Sox's ceiling in painful fashion. Chris Sale, the ace who had been magnificent all year, was roughed up in Game 1 by a Marwin González double that keyed a rally. Drew Pomeranz couldn't hold leads, and Carlos Correa's home run in Game 2 put Boston in a deep hole. The young guns — Devers with a homer in Game 3, Benintendi with a two-run shot in Game 4 — provided flickers of hope, but Craig Kimbrel's inability to protect a lead in Game 4 proved fatal. The Astros, on their way to a World Series title, dispatched Boston in three games, ending a promising season with a reminder that 93 wins and a potent offense were no match for a team operating at a higher level.

chapters.title: Unexpected Heroes, Early Wobbles
chapters.description: Boston opens the season inconsistently, with Pablo Sandoval providing an unlikely highlight while the bullpen shows early cracks.

chapters.title: Grinding Through Spring
chapters.description: Role players step up to keep Boston afloat through May and June as the team wins steadily but struggles to pull away.

chapters.title: A Stumbling July
chapters.description: Boston falls below .500 for the month as bullpen meltdowns and late-game losses pile up despite individual clutch moments.

chapters.title: August Eruption
chapters.description: An 18-9 August powered by Vázquez, Betts, Moreland, Devers, and Núñez transforms Boston into a true division contender.

chapters.title: Closing Strong in September
chapters.description: Boston goes 17-10 in September, clinching the division behind timely hitting from Benintendi and Betts.

chapters.title: October's Harsh Lesson
chapters.description: The Red Sox fight but ultimately fall to the Astros in the ALDS, as clutch moments from Devers and Benintendi cannot overcome Houston's dominance.
